svg.aria-label: Diagram: regional external and internal Application Load Balancers in Google Cloud; these are Envoy-based rather than Google Front End based, so the proxy-only subnet stops being a prerequisite and becomes the data path, with every internal Application Load Balancer in a region and network sharing one subnet, backends receiving connections from it, cross-region and regional load balancers unable to share subnets because their purposes differ, and the load balancer's own virtual address living outside it; the mode is chosen once and cannot be edited, so changing between cross-region and regional means deleting and recreating; cross-region is always globally accessible with global backends and cross-region failover, while regional is not globally accessible by default, serves only same-region backends and fails over only within its region, with global access on the forwarding rule the single flag that widens client reach; high availability for the regional external variant is built from isolation rather than from one load balancer, deploying several and steering with Cloud DNS, active-passive by failover policy or active-active by geolocation policy, with health checks that must specify exactly three source regions and can only be global, and automatic failback; and reaching an internal load balancer from a connected network brings its own rules, since peering does not share firewall rules, all internal load balancers are shared automatically with no selective exposure, a Cloud VPN gateway must sit in the load balancer's region unless global access is on, and the network's dynamic routing mode decides which routes the Envoy proxies can use
svg.title: Regional Application Load Balancers: Envoy in the data path, and a mode you cannot change
svg.text: #104’s front ends belong to Google. These proxies run in your subnet, on your routes,
shared with every other Envoy load balancer in the region.
The proxy-only subnet is no longer a prerequisite. It is the data path.
“Backend VMs or endpoints of ALL internal Application Load Balancers in a region and VPC network
receive connections FROM THE PROXY-ONLY SUBNET.” So the source address cannot tell you which
load balancer sent the request — only that some Envoy LB in that region did.
“Proxy-only subnets are only used for Envoy proxies, NOT your backends.” And the load balancer’s
own VIP “is NOT located in the proxy-only subnet” — it comes from an ordinary subnet.
“Cross-region and regional load balancers CANNOT SHARE the same subnets.” Different purposes:
GLOBAL_MANAGED_PROXY vs REGIONAL_MANAGED_PROXY. Two subnets per region if you run both.
The mode is a one-time decision
“After you create a load balancer, you CAN’T EDIT ITS MODE. Instead, you must DELETE the load
balancer and CREATE A NEW ONE.”
Regional → cross-region is not a migration, it is a rebuild: new forwarding rule, new VIP unless
you reserved a static one, and a DNS change. Decide scope before you create it.
Cross-region versus regional, internal
CROSS-REGION — “ALWAYS globally accessible.” Global backends, “any region”. Failover to
healthy backends “in the same OR DIFFERENT regions”. VIPs in several regions can share one
global backend service.
REGIONAL — “NOT globally accessible by default.” Backends must be “in the same region as the
PROXY”. Failover within the region only.
Telling them apart in the console: if the REGION COLUMN IS BLANK, it is cross-region.
Regional EXTERNAL high availability: isolation, plus Cloud DNS
There is no global mode here. HA is built by deploying SEVERAL regional load balancers, because
they are “isolated from each other” and from global and classic infrastructure in the same region.
ACTIVE-PASSIVE → Cloud DNS FAILOVER routing policy. ACTIVE-ACTIVE → GEOLOCATION policy.
The steering is #97’s Cloud DNS, not a load balancer feature.
“You must specify EXACTLY THREE source regions when you create the health check”, and “ONLY
GLOBAL health checks can specify source regions.” Not two, not four. Three.
Every LB needs “the same traffic management and security configurations”. Failback is automatic.
Reaching an internal LB from a connected network
NO SELECTIVE EXPOSURE: “You cannot selectively share only SOME … internal Application Load
Balancers by using VPC Network Peering. ALL internal load balancers are shared automatically.”
Peer the network and you have exposed every one of them.
“Google Cloud firewall rules aren’t shared among networks when using VPC Network Peering” —
#81 again: you must write ingress rules for the peer’s clients yourself.
Over Cloud VPN: the gateway and tunnels must be IN THE LB’S REGION unless global access is on.
And #84 comes back: “the DYNAMIC ROUTING MODE determines which custom dynamic routes are
available to proxies in the proxy-only subnet.” Regional mode can starve the proxies.
Two frontend details that differ from #104’s global: clients “must use HTTP version 1.1 OR LATER”
— HTTP/1.0 is accepted globally and refused here. And one port per forwarding rule still holds,
but several rules may SHARE ONE VIP and one target proxy, provided IP + port + protocol is unique.
Reserve the VIP as a static address, or a delete-and-recreate changes it and your DNS with it.
